title: Descriptor: 5G Open Radio Access Network Multi-Modal Intrusion Detection Dataset (NetsLab-5GORAN-IDD)
authors: Abed Zadeh F.; Civciss A.; Wickrama Arachchilage V. R.; Liyanage M.; Sandeepa C.
open_source_code: dataset only; CC-BY-4.0; 16.85 GB total per the Zenodo API (Benign.zip 5.94GB, DoS.zip 3.47GB, DDOS.zip 3.09GB, BruteForce.zip 3.32GB, Web.zip 0.59GB; Network_Dataset.csv 227.2MB; Network_Dataset.db 210.7MB; Lower_Layer_Data.db 5.4MB). NOTE: the description lists six categories but only five zips are published - Probe.zip is ABSENT
testbed: physical 5G O-RAN testbed, University College Dublin; Dell Precision 7920 O-Cloud edge server; 2 physical UEs
ric_type: RIC present; DU radio metrics exported over the E2 interface
attack_types: Benign; DoS; DDoS; Probe; Brute Force; Web attacks
feature_modalities: CU packet/flow (raw .pcap + Zeek conn.log/http.log/files.log) AND DU radio telemetry (22 PHY/MAC metrics per record, .txt)

title: Cross-Layer Intrusion Detection in 5G O-RAN: Gains and Limits of Fusing Radio Telemetry with Network Flow Records
authors: Fard H.; Komarov I.; Wunder G.
venue: IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience (CSR), Lisbon
testbed: uses the UCD corpus (no new testbed)
attack_types: as per corpus; DoS emphasised in the confusion analysis
feature_modalities: DU radio telemetry; CU network flow records; fusion of both
model: seven architectures including GRU and Transformer
baseline_models: single-modality variants of the same architectures
false_alert_evaluation: partial - reports a 1% FPR operating point, but no alert volume and no base-rate sweep
limitations: persistent 27-46% DoS-to-Benign confusion, which the authors attribute to windowed statistical aggregation rather than model capacity
relevance: CRITICAL - nearest prior work on our D_A; sets the in-distribution reference and constrains our novelty
what_our_project_learns: (i) run-disjoint splitting on this corpus is the established protocol, so a random split would be indefensible; (ii) radio features match or beat flow features IN-DISTRIBUTION, which is the first half of our H4 sign-flip and is now prior work; (iii) their windowing causes heavy DoS/Benign confusion, so our windowing policy (A12) must be justified against it
potential_gap: fusion gains measured in-distribution only. Cross-deployment transfer, tail latency, resource cost, alert burden, calibration and robustness are all absent. The second half of our H4 (radio features HURT transfer) is untested by them
verification_status: PARTIAL: arXiv abstract page retrieved; full text NOT read

title: Enabling Real-Time AI in O-RAN: Deploying and Measuring AI Inside a Near-RT RIC xApp
authors: Obiuwevwi L.; Rechowicz K. J.; Jayarathna S.; Bouk S. H.; Afrin F.; Barati C. N.; Moghim N.; Nanou V.; Rahman M. E.; Shetty S.
ric_type: FlexRIC (real Near-RT RIC, model embedded in the xApp)
attack_types: none - network-state classification, not intrusion detection
feature_modalities: cross-layer RAN state: MAC, RLC, PDCP, GTP, UE count
model: logistic regression and shallow MLP exported as deterministic C inference modules, no external ML runtime
baseline_models: the two models compared against each other
latency_evaluation: yes - inference-only 1-5 us (LR) and 10-25 us (MLP); end-to-end below 4 ms; CDF characterisation plus a noise ablation
p95_latency: yes - more than 95% of projected loop executions within the 10 ms budget
limitations: the authors state the work validates embedding and execution feasibility rather than production-level generalisation; accuracy only 0.88-0.90; synthetic data
relevance: CRITICAL - the strongest existing latency comparator, and it assumes the same B = 10 ms budget we do
what_our_project_learns: (i) our 10 ms budget has independent precedent; (ii) a C-exported linear model runs orders of magnitude faster than our assumed per-decision cost, so our latency finding must concern the FULL pipeline (feature construction and serialisation), not inference, or it is already answered; (iii) they report p95 but NOT p99, so the tail is still open
potential_gap: no p99, no CPU/RAM, no throughput sweep, no real attack data, no detection-quality/latency trade-off
verification_status: PARTIAL: arXiv abstract page retrieved; full text NOT read

title: Performance Analysis of an AI-Based IDS xApp for Cyberattack Anomaly Detection in O-RAN Near-RT RIC
venue: ScienceDirect (Tech Science Press host), article S152614922600202X
dataset: NetsLab-5GORAN-IDD (O-CU network layer plus O-DU radio telemetry)
ric_type: deployed in a Near-RT RIC environment (claimed)
feature_modalities: O-CU network layer and O-DU radio telemetry
model: LSTM, CNN, Transformer, Autoencoder; a structurally optimised LSTM is selected
latency_evaluation: yes - peak inference around 600 ms (LSTM, CNN) and 850 ms (Autoencoder); stress test to 80,000 instances
limitations: assumes a 1000 ms near-RT budget, the permissive end of the 10 ms - 1 s range; F1 94.87% (O-CU) and 99.49% (O-DU) are in-distribution only
relevance: HIGH - a second latency comparator on the same corpus, reaching the OPPOSITE deployability verdict to P04 purely by choosing a different budget
what_our_project_learns: the near-RT budget is a RANGE (10 ms to 1 s), not a constant, so a single-value budget makes the deployability verdict an authoring choice. We must sweep B rather than assert B = 10 ms
potential_gap: single budget value; no cross-deployment evaluation; percentile methodology not established from the retrieved text
verification_status: WEAK: publisher returned HTTP 403; fields come from search-result snippets only. MUST be re-verified before citation

venue: ACM Transactions on Information and System Security (TISSEC) 3(3)
feature_modalities: n/a
